title: Chapter 44
paragraphs: Elinor recoiled at the sight of him, her face filled with horror. Following her first impulse, she immediately turned to leave. Her hand was already on the door handle when he hurried towards her and stopped her with a voice that sounded more like an order than a plea.
“Miss Dashwood, stay for half an hour—for ten minutes. I beg you.”
“No, sir,” she answered firmly. “I shall _not_ stay. You can have no business with _me_. I suppose the servants neglected to tell you that Mr. Palmer is away.”
“If they had told me that Mr. Palmer and every relation he has were at the devil,” he exclaimed vehemently, “I would not have turned away. My business is with you alone.”
“With me!” She was utterly astonished. “Very well, sir. Be quick, and if possible, less forceful.”
“Sit down, and I shall do both.”

She hesitated, uncertain what to do. She thought of Colonel Brandon arriving and finding her there. Yet she had promised to listen, and her curiosity was engaged as well as her honour. After a moment she decided that prudence required speed, and that agreeing would best secure it. She silently approached the table and sat down. He took the chair opposite. For half a minute neither spoke.
“Please be quick, sir,” Elinor said impatiently. “I have no time that I can spare.”
He sat absorbed in deep thought and seemed not to hear what she said.
“Your sister is out of danger,” he said abruptly a moment later. “The servant told me. Thank God! But is it true? Is it really true?”
Elinor would not answer. He repeated the question with even greater urgency.
“For God's sake, tell me! Is she out of danger or not?”
“We hope she is.”
He got up and walked across the room.

“If I had known that half an hour ago! But since I _am_ here”—he returned to his chair with forced liveliness—“what does it matter? For once, Miss Dashwood, perhaps for the last time, let us be cheerful together. I am in an excellent mood for gaiety. Tell me honestly”—his cheeks flushed more deeply—“do you think me more a villain or a fool?”

Elinor looked at him in greater astonishment than ever. She began to suspect he was drunk. Neither this strange visit nor his strange behaviour seemed otherwise explicable. Believing that, she immediately rose and said,
“Mr. Willoughby, I advise you to return to Combe for now. I cannot spare any more time. Whatever business you have with me, you will remember and explain it better tomorrow.”
“I understand,” he answered with a meaningful smile, his voice perfectly steady. “Yes, I am very drunk. A pint of porter with my cold beef at Marlborough was enough to overcome me.”
“At Marlborough!” Elinor exclaimed, increasingly unable to understand what he was trying to say.
“Yes. I left London at eight this morning. The only ten minutes I have spent outside my carriage since then gave me a bite to eat at Marlborough.”

The steadiness of his manner and the intelligence in his eyes convinced Elinor that, whatever other inexcusable folly had brought him to Cleveland, drunkenness had not. After a moment's consideration, she said,

“Mr. Willoughby, you _ought_ to feel, as I certainly _do_, that after everything that has happened, coming here like this and forcing your presence on me needs a very particular excuse. What do you intend by it?”

“I intend,” he said with serious intensity, “if possible, to make you hate me a little less than you do _now_. I want to offer some explanation, some apology for the past, to lay my whole heart before you. If I can persuade you that, though I have always been an idiot, I have not always been a scoundrel, perhaps I may gain something like forgiveness from Ma—from your sister.”
“Is that really why you have come here?”
“Upon my soul, it is.” His warmth recalled the former Willoughby so vividly that, against her will, she began to believe him sincere.
“If that is all, you can be satisfied already. Marianne _does_ forgive you. She has forgiven you for a _long_ time.”
“Has she?” he cried as eagerly as before. “Then she forgave me before she should have. But she shall forgive me again, and with better reason. Will you listen to me _now_?”
Elinor bowed to show her agreement.

“I don't know,” he said after a pause in which she waited and he reflected, “how _you_ have explained my behaviour to your sister, or what monstrous motive you have assigned me. Perhaps you will think no better of me, but it is worth trying, and you shall hear everything. When I first became close to your family, I had no purpose beyond spending the time pleasantly while I had to remain in Devonshire—more pleasantly than I ever had before. Your sister's beauty and engaging manner naturally attracted me. Her behaviour towards me almost from the beginning was such—it astonishes me now, when I remember what it was, and what _she_ was, that my heart could have remained so untouched. But I must admit that at first it merely flattered my vanity. I did not consider her happiness, only my own amusement. Yielding to feelings I had always indulged too freely, I used every means I could to make her like me, without intending to return her love.”
At this point, Elinor turned her eyes on him with the angriest contempt and stopped him by saying,

“Mr. Willoughby, there is hardly any further point in your continuing this account, or in my listening to it. Nothing that follows can excuse such a beginning. Please spare me the pain of hearing any more about the matter.”

“I insist that you hear it all,” he replied. “My fortune was never large, and I had always spent extravagantly, always mixed with people richer than myself. Every year since I came of age—and probably before—had increased my debts. My old cousin Mrs. Smith's death was to free me, but that was uncertain and might be far off. For some time I had therefore intended to repair my finances by marrying a wealthy woman. Loving your sister was out of the question. With a pettiness, selfishness, and cruelty which no angry or contemptuous look, even yours, Miss Dashwood, can condemn too much, I tried to win her affection without any thought of returning it. One thing may be said for me: even in that dreadful state of selfish vanity, I did not understand the full harm I planned, because _then_ I did not know what love was. But have I ever known? You may well doubt it. If I had truly loved, could I have sacrificed my feelings to vanity and greed? Still worse, could I have sacrificed hers? Yet I did. To escape a relative poverty which her love and company would have stripped of every terror, I made myself rich and lost everything that could make wealth a blessing.”
“Then you did once believe yourself in love with her?” Elinor asked, a little softened.

“Who could have resisted such attractions, such tenderness? Is there a man alive who could? Yes, little by little, without noticing, I became sincerely attached. The happiest hours of my life were those I spent with her knowing my intentions were honourable and my feelings innocent. Even _then_, though fully determined to propose, I wrongly allowed myself to postpone it day after day. I disliked committing myself while my finances were so troubled. I won't argue the point, or wait for _you_ to explain the absurdity—and worse than absurdity—of hesitating to give my word when my honour was already pledged. Events have proved me a calculating fool, carefully preserving an opportunity to make myself contemptible and miserable for ever. At last, though, I made up my mind. As soon as I could find her alone, I would justify my constant attentions and openly declare the love I had already taken such pains to display. But in the interval, in the few hours before I could speak to her privately, something happened—an unlucky event that destroyed my resolution and all my happiness. A discovery was made.” He hesitated and looked down. “Mrs. Smith had somehow been told, I suppose by a distant relation interested in depriving me of her favour, about an affair, a connection—but I needn't explain further.” He looked at Elinor, his colour rising, his eyes questioning. “Your close acquaintance—you have probably known the whole story for some time.”

“I have,” Elinor answered, colouring too and hardening her heart again against pity. “I have heard everything. I confess I cannot understand how you could explain away any part of your guilt in that dreadful affair.”

“Remember who told you,” Willoughby cried. “Could his account be impartial? I admit I should have respected her position and her character. I am not trying to justify myself. But I cannot let you suppose I have nothing to say, that because she was wronged she was beyond reproach, or that because _I_ was dissolute, _she_ must be a saint. The violence of her passions, the weakness of her understanding—but I do not mean to defend myself. Her love deserved better treatment. I often remember with deep self-reproach the tenderness that briefly made me feel something in return. I wish, sincerely, that it had never happened. But she is not the only person I have hurt. I have hurt someone whose love for me—may I say it?—was scarcely less warm, and whose mind was infinitely superior!”

“Your indifference towards that unfortunate girl is no excuse for cruelly abandoning her. I must say it, however unpleasant such a subject is to discuss. Do not imagine that any weakness or natural lack of understanding on her part excuses the deliberate cruelty so clear on yours. You must have known that while you enjoyed yourself in Devonshire, pursuing new schemes, always cheerful and happy, she had been reduced to utter poverty.”
“But I swear I did _not_ know,” he answered heatedly. “I had forgotten that I neglected to give her my address. And ordinary common sense might have shown her how to discover it.”
“Well, sir, what did Mrs. Smith say to you?”

“She accused me directly, and you can imagine my embarrassment. Her pure life, rigid ideas, ignorance of the world—everything was against me. I could not deny the facts, and every attempt to soften them failed. I think she was already inclined to question my conduct generally. She was also displeased by how little attention and time I had given her during this visit. In short, it ended in a complete break. I could have saved myself in one way. At the height of her morality, the good woman offered to forgive everything if I married Eliza. That was impossible, and she formally dismissed me from both her favour and her house. I was to leave the next morning. I spent the night considering what to do. The struggle was great, but ended too soon. My love for Marianne, my certainty that she loved me, could not outweigh my fear of poverty or overcome my false belief that wealth was necessary—a belief to which I was naturally inclined and which extravagant company had strengthened. I had reason to believe my present wife would accept me if I proposed, and persuaded myself that ordinary prudence left no other course. But a painful scene awaited me before I could leave Devonshire. I was due to dine with you that very day and had to offer some apology for cancelling. I debated for a long time whether to write it or deliver it myself. Seeing Marianne would be dreadful. I even doubted whether I could see her again and keep my resolution. In that respect, however, I underestimated my own greatness of spirit, as events proved. I went, saw her, saw her miserable, left her miserable—and left hoping never to see her again.”
“Why did you call, Mr. Willoughby?” Elinor asked reproachfully. “A note would have served every purpose. Why did you need to come yourself?”

“My pride required it. I could not bear to leave in a way that might make you or the neighbours suspect any part of what had happened between Mrs. Smith and me. I therefore decided to call at the cottage on my way to Honiton. But seeing your dear sister was truly dreadful. To make it worse, I found her alone; the rest of you had gone somewhere, I don't know where. Only the previous evening I had left her absolutely determined to do right. Within a few hours she was to be engaged to me for ever. I remember how happy and cheerful I felt walking back from the cottage to Allenham, pleased with myself and delighted with everyone. Yet in this last friendly meeting I approached her so guilty that I could hardly pretend otherwise. Her sorrow, her disappointment, her deep distress when I said I must leave Devonshire immediately—I shall never forget it. And all combined with such trust, such confidence in me! Oh God, what a heartless scoundrel I was!”
For a few moments they were both silent. Elinor spoke first.
“Did you tell Marianne that you would return soon?”

“I don't know what I told her,” he answered impatiently. “Certainly less than the past deserved, and probably much more than the future justified. I cannot think about it. I cannot. Then your dear mother came to torment me further with all her kindness and trust. Thank heaven it _did_ torment me. I was miserable. Miss Dashwood, you cannot imagine the comfort I find in remembering my misery. I resent myself so bitterly for the stupid, wicked foolishness of my heart that all the suffering it caused me is now a source of triumph and satisfaction. Well, I left everything I loved and went to people towards whom I felt, at best, indifference. The journey to London, using my own horses and therefore moving so slowly, with nobody to speak to! Such cheerful thoughts; such delightful prospects when I looked ahead; such a soothing picture when I looked back towards Barton! Oh, it was a blessed journey.”
He fell silent.
“Well, sir,” Elinor said, pitying him but increasingly impatient for him to leave, “is that everything you have to say?”
“Everything? No. Have you forgotten what happened in London? That infamous letter? Did Marianne show it to you?”
“Yes. I saw every note exchanged between you.”

“When her first letter reached me—which it did immediately, because I had been in London all along—what I felt was, in the usual phrase, beyond expression. More simply, perhaps too simply to move anyone, my feelings were very, very painful. Every line and word was a dagger to my heart, to use a worn-out metaphor its dear writer would forbid if she were here. The news that Marianne was in London struck like a thunderbolt. Thunderbolts and daggers! How she would have rebuked me! Her tastes and opinions are, I believe, better known to me than my own, and certainly dearer.”
Elinor's heart had changed repeatedly through this extraordinary conversation, and softened again now. Yet she felt obliged to check the kind of thoughts he had just expressed.
“This is wrong, Mr. Willoughby. Remember that you are married. Tell me only what you honestly believe I need to hear.”

“Marianne's note assured me that I was as dear to her as ever. Despite our many weeks apart, her feelings had not changed, and she trusted mine as completely as before. It woke all my remorse. I say woke, because time, London, business, and pleasure had partly quieted it. I was becoming a fine hardened villain, imagining I no longer cared for her and choosing to suppose she no longer cared for me. I told myself our attachment had been an idle, trivial affair, and shrugged my shoulders to prove it. I silenced every reproach and overcame every scruple by occasionally telling myself, ‘I shall be heartily glad to hear she has married well.’ Her note made me understand myself better. I knew she was infinitely dearer to me than any other woman, and that I was treating her shamefully. But everything between Miss Grey and me was just settled. I could not retreat. I could only avoid you both. I sent Marianne no answer, hoping to prevent any further notice from her. For a while I even decided not to call in Berkeley Street. At last I thought it wiser to behave like a cool, ordinary acquaintance. One morning I watched until you were all safely out, then left my card.”
“You watched until we had left the house?”

“Exactly. You would be surprised how often I watched you, and how often I nearly met you. Many times I went into a shop to avoid being seen as your carriage passed. Living in Bond Street, I scarcely went a day without glimpsing one of you. Only constant vigilance and an unchanging determination to keep out of sight could have separated us so long. I avoided the Middletons as far as possible, and anyone else likely to be a mutual acquaintance. But not knowing they were in London, I stumbled into Sir John, I think on his first day, and the day after I called at Mrs. Jennings's. He invited me to a dance that evening. Even if he had _not_ mentioned you and Marianne as an attraction, I should have been too certain you would be there to venture near him. The next morning came another note from Marianne, still loving, open, innocent, trusting—everything that made _my_ behaviour most hateful. I could not answer. I tried, but could not form a sentence. Yet I think I thought of her every moment of the day. If you _can_ pity me, Miss Dashwood, pity my position _then_. With my head and heart full of your sister, I had to act the happy lover to another woman. Those three or four weeks were the worst of all. At last, as you know, I was forced to meet you. What a fine figure I made! What an evening of agony! Marianne, lovely as an angel, on one side, calling me Willoughby in that voice! Oh God, holding out her hand, asking for an explanation, those beautiful eyes fixed so anxiously and eloquently on my face! And Sophia on the other side, jealous as the devil, looking all that—well, it doesn't matter. It is over. Such an evening! I escaped as soon as I could, but not before I saw Marianne's dear face white as death. _That_ was the last, the very last sight I had of her. That is how I last saw her. It was dreadful. Yet today, thinking she was really dying, I found a sort of comfort in believing I knew exactly how she would appear to the last people to see her alive. All through my journey she was before me, constantly, with that same expression and colour.”
They paused briefly, each absorbed in thought. Willoughby roused himself first and broke the silence.
“Well, I must be quick and go. Your sister is certainly better, certainly out of danger?”
“We have been assured she is.”
“And your poor mother, so devoted to Marianne!”
“But your letter, Mr. Willoughby—your own letter. Have you anything to explain about that?”

“Yes, yes, _that_ especially. As you know, your sister wrote again the very next morning. You saw her words. I was breakfasting at the Ellisons', and her letter came there from my lodgings with several others. Sophia noticed it before I did. Its size, the fine paper, and the handwriting immediately made her suspicious. She had already heard some vague report that I was attached to a young woman in Devonshire. What she saw the previous evening identified the woman and increased her jealousy. Adopting a playful manner, so delightful in a woman one loves, she immediately opened and read it. Her impudence was well rewarded: what she read made her miserable. I could have endured her misery, but her rage, her malice—those had to be soothed at any cost. In short, what do you think of my wife's letter-writing style? Delicate, tender, truly feminine, wasn't it?”
“Your wife! But the letter was in your own handwriting.”

“Yes, my sole credit was obediently copying sentences I was ashamed to sign. The original was entirely hers: her happy ideas, her gentle language. But what could I do? We were engaged, everything was being prepared, the date almost fixed—but I am talking foolishly. Preparations! Dates! The plain truth is that I needed her money. In my position, I had to do anything to prevent a break. Besides, what difference did the wording make to my character in Marianne's eyes, or her friends'? The result could only be the same. My task was to declare myself a scoundrel; whether I did it with a bow or a shout mattered little. ‘I am ruined in their opinion for ever,’ I told myself. ‘I can never see them again. They already think me unprincipled; this letter will only make them think me a brute as well.’ That was how I reasoned, with a kind of desperate recklessness, while copying my wife's words and parting with the last reminders of Marianne. Her three notes were, unfortunately, all in my pocketbook. Otherwise I would have denied having them and treasured them for ever. I had to pack them up without even kissing them. And the lock of hair, which I had always carried in the same pocketbook—Madam was now searching it with the most charming spite—that dear lock too. Everything, every keepsake, was torn from me.”

“You are very wrong, Mr. Willoughby, very much to blame,” Elinor said, though her voice betrayed compassion despite herself. “You should not speak like this about either your wife or my sister. You made your choice; nobody forced it upon you. Your wife has a right to your courtesy, at least to your respect. She must care for you, or she would not have married you. Treating her unkindly and speaking contemptuously of her does nothing to make amends to Marianne. Nor can I imagine it eases your own conscience.”

“Do not speak to me of my wife,” he said with a deep sigh. “She does not deserve your pity. She knew I did not love her when we married. Well, we married, went to Combe Magna to be happy, and then returned to London to enjoy ourselves. Now do you pity me, Miss Dashwood? Or has all this been useless? Am I even a little less guilty in your eyes than before? My intentions were not always bad. Have I explained away any part of my guilt?”

“Yes, certainly something—a little. You have shown yourself less blameworthy on the whole than I believed. Your heart has proved less wicked, much less wicked. But I hardly know—the misery you have caused—I can scarcely imagine what could have made it worse.”

“When your sister recovers, will you repeat what I have told you? Let me be a little less condemned in her opinion as well as yours. You say she has already forgiven me. Let me imagine that knowing more of my heart and my feelings now might bring a more spontaneous, natural, gentle, less dignified forgiveness. Tell her how miserable and repentant I am. Tell her my heart never changed towards her, and, if you will, that she is dearer to me at this moment than ever.”
“I shall tell her everything necessary to what we may comparatively call your defence. But you have not explained why you came at this particular time, or how you heard she was ill.”

“Last night I met Sir John Middleton in the lobby at Drury Lane. Recognising me, he spoke for the first time in two months. I had noticed without surprise or resentment that he had ignored me since my marriage. But now his kind, honest, foolish soul was so full of anger with me and concern for Marianne that he could not resist telling me something he knew ought to hurt me terribly, though he probably doubted that it _would_. As bluntly as possible, he said Marianne Dashwood was dying of a putrid fever at Cleveland. A letter received that morning from Mrs. Jennings described her danger as extreme; the Palmers had all fled in fright, and so on. I was too shocked to pretend indifference even to someone as unobservant as Sir John. Seeing my suffering softened his heart. So much resentment disappeared that, when we parted, he nearly shook my hand while reminding me of an old promise about a pointer puppy. What I felt on hearing your sister was dying—dying while she believed me the greatest villain alive, despising and hating me in her final moments, for how could I know what dreadful intentions I had been accused of? I knew _one_ person would paint me capable of anything. What I felt was terrible. I quickly decided what to do, and at eight this morning I was in my carriage. Now you know everything.”

Elinor made no reply. Her thoughts fixed silently on the irreparable damage that independence granted too young, with its habits of idleness, dissipation, and luxury, had done to this man's mind, character, and happiness. He combined every advantage of looks and ability with a naturally open, honest disposition and a sensitive, affectionate heart. Society had made him extravagant and vain; extravagance and vanity had made him cold and selfish. Seeking a guilty triumph over someone else's feelings, vanity had drawn him into genuine love. Extravagance, or its child necessity, had then demanded the sacrifice of that love. Every fault that led him into wrongdoing had also led him to punishment. The attachment from which he had outwardly torn himself, against honour, feeling, and every better interest, now ruled his thoughts when it was no longer permissible. The marriage for which he had so readily abandoned Marianne to misery would probably bring him unhappiness far less curable than hers. After several minutes, Willoughby recalled her from these reflections. Emerging from thoughts at least as painful, he sprang up to leave and said,
“There is no point in remaining here. I must go.”
“Are you returning to London now?”
“No, to Combe Magna. I have business there, then London in a day or two. Goodbye.”
He offered his hand. She could not refuse her own, and he pressed it affectionately.
“And you _do_ think a little better of me?” he asked, releasing her hand and leaning against the mantelpiece as though forgetting he meant to leave.

Elinor assured him she did: she forgave him, pitied him, wished him well, and even cared about his happiness. She added some gentle advice about the conduct most likely to secure it. His answer offered little encouragement.

“As for that,” he said, “I must struggle through the world as best I can. Happiness at home is impossible. But if I may believe that you and your family care about my fate and actions, perhaps it may help, perhaps keep me on my guard. At least it may give me something to live for. Marianne is certainly lost to me for ever. Even if some blessed chance left me free again—”
Elinor interrupted him with a rebuke.
“Well,” he answered, “goodbye once more. Now I shall go away and live in fear of one event.”
“What do you mean?”
“Your sister getting married.”
“You are very wrong. She can never be more completely lost to you than she is already.”

“But she will be gained by someone else. And if that person is the very man I could least bear—but I shall not stay and destroy your compassion by showing that I forgive least where I have wronged most. Goodbye. God bless you!”
With those words, he hurried from the room almost at a run.
